string-array.name: municipalities_array
string-array.item: Beijing is the capital of China and one of its four municipalities administered directly by the central government. Its imperial history is visible in the Forbidden City, which housed Ming and Qing emperors. The Temple of Heaven preserves ceremonial buildings where emperors prayed for good harvests. The Summer Palace combines gardens, lakes and palace architecture, while sections of the Great Wall lie in the surrounding mountains. Today, Beijing brings together government institutions, universities, museums and modern transport. Visitors can explore historic neighbourhoods alongside contemporary districts, making the city an important place to understand the political and cultural development of China.

Shanghai is a municipality on the eastern coast of China, near the mouth of the Yangtze River. The settlement became a county in 1292 and opened as a treaty port in 1843, important stages in its growth as a commercial city. Historic buildings along the Bund face the modern skyline of Pudong across the Huangpu River. Shanghai is also known for its Haipai culture, which combines local traditions with influences from outside China. Museums, gardens and old neighbourhoods preserve different parts of this history. Today, the city is an important centre for finance, trade, shipping and international cultural exchange.

Chongqing is a municipality in southwest China on the upper reaches of the Yangtze River. Its central urban area developed around the meeting of the Yangtze and Jialing rivers, where steep hills and waterways shape the city. Chongqing became a municipality directly under the central government in 1997. The wider municipal area includes urban districts, smaller cities and mountainous countryside. Jiefangbei reflects its commercial development, while Ciqikou preserves traditional streets and local cultural heritage. Bridges, railways and the Yangtze River cableway connect different parts of the urban landscape. These geographical and historical features explain its familiar identity as a mountain city.

Tianjin is a municipality in northern China beside the Haihe River and the Bohai Sea. A garrison established in 1404 gave the city an important place in the transport and defence of the capital region. Connections with the Grand Canal and coastal shipping helped it develop as a trading centre. Its modern history also includes the opening of a treaty port in 1860 and the development of foreign concession areas. European-style buildings remain visible in districts such as the Italian Style Area. Today, riverfront walks, museums and a major seaport connect this historical inheritance with the contemporary life of the city.
